source_text: Καὶ γὰρ ἐγώ, μαθὼν περίβλημα πονηρὸν εἰς ἀποστροφὴν τῶν ἄλλων ἀνθρώπων περιτεθειμένον ὑπὸ τῶν φαύλων δαιμόνων τοῖς Χριστιανῶν θείοις διδάγμασι, καὶ ψευδολογουμένων ταῦτα καὶ τοῦ περιβλήματος κατεγέλασα καὶ τῆς παρὰ τοῖς πολλοῖς δόξης. Χριστιανὸς εὑρεθῆναι καὶ εὐχόμενος καὶ παμμάχως ἀγωνιζόμενος ὁμολογῶ, οἰχ ὅτι ἀλλότριά ἐστι τὰ Πλάτωνος διδάγματα τοῦ Χριστοῦ, ἀλλ᾿ ὅτι οὐκ ἔστι πάντη ὅμοια, ὥσπερ οὐδὲ τὰ τῶν ἄλλων, Στωϊκῶν τε καὶ ποιητῶν καὶ συγγραφέων. Ἕκαστος γάρ τις ἀπὸ μέρους τοῦ σπερματικοῦ θείου λόγου τὸ συγγενὲς ὁρῶν καλῶς ἐφθέγξατο· οἱ δὲ τἀναντία ἑαυτοῖς ἐν κυριωτέροις εἰρηκότες οὐκ ἐπιστήμην τὴν ἄπτωτον καὶ γνῶσιν τὴν ἀνέλεγκτον φαίνονται ἐσχηκέναι. Ὅσα οὖν παρὰ καλῶς εἴρηται, ἡμῶν τᾶν Χριστιανῶν ἐστι· τὸν γὰρ ἀπὸ ἀγεννήτου καὶ ἀῤῥήτου θεοῦ λόγον μετὰ τὸν θεὸν προσκυνοῦμεν καὶ ἀγαπῶμεν, ἐπειδὴ καὶ δι᾿ ἡμᾶς ἄνθρωπος γέγονεν, ὅπως καὶ τῶν παθῶν τῶν ἡμετέρων συμμέτοχος γενόμενος καὶ ἴασιν ποιήσηται. Οἱ γὰρ συγγραφεῖς πάντες διὰ τῆς ἐνούσης ἐμφύτου τοῦ λόγου σπορᾶς ἀμυδρῶς ἐδύναντο ὁρᾶν τὰ ὄντα. Ἕτερον γάρ ἐστι σπέρμα τινὸς καὶ μίμημα κατὰ δύναμιν δοθέν, καὶ ἕτερον αὐτό, οὗ κατὰ χάριν τὴν ἀπ᾿ ἐκείνου ἡ μετουσία καὶ μίμησις γίνεται.
thought_title: Justin Martyr's View on Christian Doctrine
pass_a_gloss: For I, having learned that an evil cloak has been placed on the divine teachings of the Christians by the evil demons for the apostasy of the other men, and that these things are being falsely spoken and the cloak is being ridiculed and the reputation among the many, I confess that I have been found to be a Christian and I am praying and struggling in every way. Because the teachings of Plato are foreign to the teachings of Christ, not because they are not similar in every way, just like the teachings of the Stoics and poets and writers are not. For each one, seeing the kinship of the divine seed word, spoke well from a part. But those who have spoken contrary things to themselves in more authoritative matters do not seem to have had untainted knowledge and unrefuted understanding. Therefore, whatever has been spoken well is ours, the Christians'; for we worship and love the Word who is from the unbegotten and unspoken God, after God, since He also became human for our sake, so that having become a partaker of our passions, He may bring about a cure. For all writers were able to see the things that are, dimly, through the innate seed of the word that is in them. For one thing is the seed of something and an imitation given according to power, and another is the actual thing, by which the participation and imitation according to grace from it come about.
pass_b_english: I have learned that evil demons have thrown a wicked cloak over the divine teachings of the Christians in order to drive other people away from them; because these things are being falsely spoken, I have laughed both at the cloak itself and at the reputation it enjoys among the many. I confess that I have been found to be a Christian, and I pray and struggle in every way. The teachings of Plato are foreign to the teachings of Christ, not because they are entirely unlike them, just as the teachings of the Stoics and poets and writers are not entirely unlike them. For each person, seeing the kinship of the divine seed Word, spoke well from a part. But those who have spoken things contrary to themselves in more authoritative matters do not appear to possess untainted knowledge and unrefuted understanding. Therefore, whatever has been spoken well belongs to us Christians. For we worship and love the Word who is from the unbegotten and unutterable God, after God, since He also became human for our sake, so that by becoming a partaker of our passions He may bring about a cure. For all writers were able to see the things that are, dimly, through the innate seed of the Word that is in them. For one thing is a seed of something and an imitation given according to power, and another is the thing itself, by which the participation and imitation according to grace from it come about.

review.notes: Pass A fails to translate the verb 'κατεγέλασα' (I ridiculed/laughed at) correctly in relation to the objects, instead rendering it as 'the cloak is being ridiculed', which changes the agency from the author to the cloak itself. Furthermore, Pass A misinterprets the causal/concessive structure of the sentence 'οὐκ ἔστι πάντη ὅμοια' (they are not entirely alike), translating it as 'not because they are not similar', which reverses the logic of the comparison. Pass B is a much more accurate translation of the Greek.
reasons: Pass A misrepresents agency: 'κατεγέλασα καὶ τῆς παρὰ τοῖς πολλοῖς δόξης' (I ridiculed both the cloak and the reputation) is translated as 'the cloak is being ridiculed and the reputation among the many', turning a first-person active verb into a passive construction. Pass A also misrepresents the logic of the comparison: 'οὐκ ἔστι πάντη ὅμοια' (they are not entirely alike) is translated as 'not because they are not similar', which is a semantic error regarding the relationship between the clauses.

review.notes: The Greek text is correctly identified as Justin's Second Apology 13. The translation preserves the full content of the source paragraph, including all arguments, quotations, and qualifications. The title names the thought, not just a locus. No OCR damage or uncertain readings are noted. The translation accurately reflects the Greek in terms of negation, agency, modality, doctrine, and scripture. All inline citations are correct and match the quoted or alluded-to content. The translation is faithful to the source in both Pass A and Pass B.
